newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Families of detained Timor activists plan vigil.
newsitem.headline: Families of detained Timor activists plan vigil.

text.p: Twenty Malaysian human rights activists remained in jail on Tuesday three days after an aborted East Timor conference and families of the detained prepared a candlelight vigil in protest.
Family members and organisers of the conference said they planned to hold the vigil outside the police station where the activists were being held.

The vigil would commemorate the fifth anniversary on Tuesday of the killing of at least 50 demonstrators by Indonesian troops in the East Timor capital of Dili in 1991, a spokesman for the Asia Pacific Conference on East Timor 11 (APCET II) said.

Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975 and has ruled it since then in defiance of the United Nations, which has never recognised Jakarta's 1976 annexation of the territory.

The 20 detainees were among 66 Malaysian activists and journalists who were rounded up on Saturday after a mob of youths, comprising groups allied to the government, forcibly shut down the conference.
Another 46 foreign participants, including two Roman Catholic bishops, were deported.
The conference was called to draw international attention to the plight of East Timor and was condemned by Kuala Lumpur as damaging to its relations with Indonesia.
Seven of the several hundred people who stormed the conference, overturning furniture and berating the activists, were detained and released several hours later.
APCET II organisers on Tuesday renewed a call for the remaining activists' release from what it described as "appalling conditions" in the police station.
It said three of the detainees had been sent to hospital, two suffering asthma attacks.
"There is no word on the fate of the detained," APCET II said in a statement on Tuesday. "The police have been tight-lipped as to when the 20 will be released."
APCET II said the remaining detainees could be held until Thursday, when they will have to be released or have their remand periods extended.
The Malaysian Bar Council on Tuesday also expressed concern about the detainees.

"The Bar Council calls for the immediate and unconditional release of all conference organisers and participants still detained and for action to be taken against those who had resorted to unlawful action to disrupt the meeting," a statement from the legal group said.

Jomo Sundram, a Malaya University economics professor who was among those jailed and later released, urged Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad "to condemn the fascist-like actions of goons from the youth wings of the ruling coalition".
